The HTTP 200 plus blank lines shows that the server accepted the request and is holding the connection open while it waits. This is normal, documented behavior, not a server failure. If the client is HTTPX, the blank lines also explain why its default read timeout did not fire: HTTPX waits for 5 seconds of network inactivity, and each empty line counts as received data ([Timeouts - HTTPX](https://www.python-httpx.org/advanced/timeouts/)). The 75-second expiry is therefore the client’s own wall-clock deadline, not a server-sent error.

Set the overall deadline above 600 seconds plus expected generation time, for example 15 minutes, not 75 seconds. The DeepSeek server closes a connection only if inference has not started after 10 minutes ([Rate Limit & Isolation](https://api-docs.deepseek.com/quick_start/rate_limit/)). So a request can wait in the queue for most of those 10 minutes and then still need time to generate the answer. Keep a short connect timeout separate from a long read or overall timeout, so a slow queue is not mistaken for a broken connection.

To separate the remaining explanations, record whether a JSON body ever arrived on the original connection, the timestamp and gap length of every blank line, the exact connection-close time, and HTTP status codes and headers. A server close near the 10-minute mark with no JSON body means inference never started. If a second request with a longer deadline delivers a JSON body after the same blank-line pattern, that supports the short-client-deadline explanation. If the blank lines stop early without a close or a body, suspect a proxy or network layer. Retry with streaming enabled: the server then sends ': keep-alive' comments, which give a second signal about server-side progress.
